archetype.name: Playoff Team (defense-first)
archetype.definition: Seattle has brought back last year's top-ranked defense almost unchanged, and it has to drag along an offense that slipped from mid-pack to the bottom third after a quarterback change.

report.headline: Same elite defense, a much worse offense, and points that lean on takeaways
report.take:
The 2025 Seahawks went 14-3 with the league's best defense. Five games into 2026, that defense hasn't changed: -0.113 EPA allowed per play, 2nd in the league, against -0.111 and 1st last year. It ranks 2nd against both pass and rush, allows the fewest yards in football at 252.4 a game, and lets opponents convert just 29.4% of third downs. This is the same unit, playing the same way.

The offense is what changed. Sam Darnold started Week 1 and Drew Lock has started the four games since. The offense has fallen from 12th in EPA last year to 26th now. The passing game is roughly average, 17th in pass EPA. The real problem is the run game, which ranks 30th in rush EPA and 32nd in short-yardage conversion at 22.2%. The line gets beaten often: it ranks 29th in QB-hit rate allowed, and its 3.08-second time to throw is the 2nd-longest in the league. Zach Charbonnet's ACL leaves the backfield to Emanuel Wilson, who has 73 carries and no burst behind this line. Seattle still scores 26.8 points a game, 8th in the league, and that number is the misleading one. Special teams add 5.07 EPA a game (2nd), and the defense has 9 takeaways (3rd), so a lot of those points start on short fields rather than coming from sustained drives.

The record is about what the play deserves. A +5.8 point differential (5th) against 3-2 and -0.37 wins over expected suggest Seattle has been slightly unlucky, not lucky. Both losses came down to giveaways. They lost 33-31 at Washington with 3 turnovers as an 8.5-point favorite, and 32-29 to San Francisco with 4 turnovers and 5 sacks allowed. The trend under Lock is the worry. Pass EPA has gone 16.1, 5.0, -5.2, -12.0 over his four starts, and the turnovers have grown with it. The market has noticed: Seattle has been favored every week and has covered once.

Where this goes depends on whether the offense can get back to neutral. The defense alone keeps Seattle in the playoff picture. But San Francisco is 5-0 and already two games clear, and the schedule still has Kansas City, a trip to SF and two games with the Rams. A wild card is the realistic target unless the quarterback play stabilizes.

strengths.title: Last year's No. 1 defense, intact
strengths.body: Seattle allows -0.113 EPA per play, nearly identical to the league-best 2025 unit. It ranks 2nd against both pass and rush, so there is no obvious lane to attack. It also ranks 3rd on third down. Defenses with this kind of year-over-year consistency under the same coach tend to hold up, so this is the most bankable part of the team.

strengths.title: A pass rush that hits and stops big plays
strengths.body: Seattle is 2nd in QB-hit rate and 5th in pressure rate. It also allows the 2nd-lowest rate of explosive passes and ranks 3rd in EPA allowed on deep throws. Quarterbacks get hit, and they rarely get a deep shot off to make up for it. A rush this disruptive also explains how the defense has generated 9 takeaways.

strengths.title: Hidden yardage from special teams and takeaways
strengths.body: Special teams add 5.07 EPA a game, 2nd in the league. Together with 9 takeaways, that is the gap between an offense ranked 26th in EPA and one that scores at a top-eight rate. Coverage-unit value is somewhat stable. Takeaway rates swing from year to year, so expect some of this scoring boost to fade.

concerns.title: A run game that can't function
concerns.body: Seattle's rushing is 30th in EPA, 26th in stuff rate and dead last on short yardage. Yards before contact are average (15th), so the problem is not only the blocking: the backs aren't creating anything after contact either. Charbonnet is out until late October at the earliest, so expect little improvement soon. A 5.7-point lean toward the run over what the situation calls for means the offense keeps choosing its weakest play.

concerns.title: Turnovers and hits are getting worse under Lock
concerns.body: Seattle committed 7 turnovers across the two losses, and they cost both games. The line ranks 29th in QB-hit rate allowed, and the long time to throw means Lock is holding the ball in that pressure. Pass EPA has fallen for three straight weeks, bottoming out at -12.0 against SF. This looks like a real flaw in the current QB-and-line combination, not bad luck.

concerns.title: Soft underneath and in the red zone
concerns.body: The defense is elite between the 20s but ranks 26th in red-zone touchdown rate allowed and 25th in EPA on short passes. It also gives top receivers room, ranking 24th in EPA allowed per target to opposing WR1s. This is part of why a defense ranked 2nd in EPA still gives up 21 points a game. Short fields after giveaways add to it.

trend.note: The defense has been steady every week. The offense has not: pass EPA has dropped from 16.1 at Arizona to -12.0 against San Francisco, and sacks and turnovers have risen over the last two games.

nextGame.headline: Denver's secondary is gutted, and its record looks luckier than Seattle's
nextGame.body:
Denver's 3-2 record comes with a -2.8 point differential. The Broncos have won every one-score game they've played, which usually doesn't last. Their offense ranks 24th in EPA and 23rd passing, and it runs into a defense ranked 2nd at almost everything. Denver's defense is built on its pass coverage, 3rd in pass EPA allowed, but it is 28th against the run and dead last in missed-tackle rate. In theory, that gives even Seattle's poor ground game something to work with.

Availability is what pushes this toward Seattle. Denver has ruled out both starting corners, Pat Surtain II and Riley Moss, and safety Talanoa Hufanga didn't practice Monday. That strips the strength of its defense. Seattle has its own worries, though. Lock (forearm) and Jaxon Smith-Njigba (ankle) were both limited. Linebacker Drake Thomas didn't practice, and Leonard Williams is questionable. All of that comes on four days' rest after a draining loss to SF, and on the road. If Lock can't go, Darnold is the alternative, and his only start was a 13-point game.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle receivers vs. backup corners
keyMatchups.body: Even with its starters, Denver has been leaky against slot and secondary receivers. It ranks last in EPA allowed to WR3s and 31st in fantasy points allowed over average to WR2s. Without Surtain and Moss, Rashid Shaheed and Cooper Kupp should find room, and Smith-Njigba's 50 targets would be a mismatch if he plays. This is the clearest path to Seattle beating its 26th-ranked offensive EPA for a night.

keyMatchups.title: Wilson against the league's worst tacklers
keyMatchups.body: Denver misses tackles at the highest rate in the league and ranks 24th in explosive runs allowed. Seattle's backs have produced almost nothing after contact, so this is the best chance they will get to break a few runs. If it fails here, the run game is unlikely to be fixed this season.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle's rush vs. Denver's protection
keyMatchups.body: This one is strength against strength. Denver's line allows the fewest QB hits in the league and the 4th-lowest sack rate, while Seattle's rush ranks 2nd in hit rate. If Bo Nix stays clean, Denver can move the ball underneath, where Seattle's defense is weakest. If he doesn't, Denver's offense has little else to lean on.

nextGame.watch: Whether Lock's forearm lets him start, and whether Seattle protects the ball. In both losses, turnovers were the only thing that beat this defense.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense should keep playing near its current level. It has now done it for a season and five games, and that alone points to a winning record and a playoff spot. The scoring is likely to drift down. An offense ranked 26th in EPA doesn't keep scoring nearly 27 a game once takeaway luck and special-teams swings even out, especially without Charbonnet and with the line allowing this many hits. The point differential says Seattle has been slightly unlucky in the standings, which helps.

The schedule doesn't give much back. Kansas City (4-0) comes to Seattle, there's a trip to unbeaten SF, and the last three weeks include the Rams twice. The softer stretch is the home run of Chicago, Arizona, Dallas and the Giants. With SF two games ahead, the division is a long shot and a wild card is the base case.
swingFactors: Lock's health and ball security, or a switch back to Darnold
Whether the takeaway rate holds at its current pace
Charbonnet's return reviving the run game

bets.reason: Seattle has a +5.8 point differential and ranks 11th in net EPA. Denver ranks 19th, has a -2.8 differential and has won every close game. Denver's main strength, its pass defense, is missing both starting corners. The short week, the road trip and Lock's forearm keep this from being a stronger play.

Denver's offense is 24th in EPA and 23rd passing, and it faces a defense ranked 2nd overall. That defense allows the 2nd-lowest rate of explosive passes and is 3rd on third down. The implied figure is derived from the 40.5 total and 2.5 spread. The main risk is Seattle turnovers handing Denver short fields, as happened against SF.

confidence.note: Five games, a quarterback who is questionable, and a scoring rate that leans on takeaways and special teams.
